extracted.intended_audience: literate general readership of The Spectator (early-18th-century readers interested in manners, morality, and social commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essays offering prescriptive social, moral, and literary commentary on behaviour, education, fame, and manners. The pieces give maxims, examples, and anecdotes intended to instruct and entertain a broad educated public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patron-client obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: When patrons take dependants under their protection the dependants become 'a Sort of Creditors' and these debts, being 'Debts of Honour,' ought to be first discharged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patrons should have both the power and obligation to assist; clients should have merit and expectation. The author excludes worthless hangers-on and impotent or unwilling patrons from this proper reciprocal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid accepting patronage without ability to reward
rubrics_metrics.description: He who will take up another's Time and Fortune in his Service, though he has no Prospect of rewarding his Merit towards him, is as unjust as he who takes up Goods without Intention or Ability to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not bind others to service you cannot remunerate; likewise patrons who cannot or will not perform promises are culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against fruitless attendance on great men
rubrics_metrics.description: Many who pursue the favour of great persons 'lose Minutes, Hours, Days, and Years in a fruitless Attendance' and often come away discontented or ruined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe that a large proportion of dependants fail to advance; frequent examples include long delays, loss of health, or lifelong disappointment. Prefer more certain routes to advancement than servile attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour of the newly elevated
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who has attained a considerable station often immediately alters his manner of treating his friends, becoming lofty, consulting less, and quick to take offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for this by noting that elevation makes people 'giddy' and less perceptive; expect new distance from former intimates and be warned that remonstration may be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways to succeed with great people
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two Ways of doing any thing with great People: by making yourself either considerable or agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becoming 'considerable' requires living without them or concealing dependence; becoming 'agreeable' means conforming to their taste and pleasures. The latter is described as the more servile option unless it matches one's natural humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of becoming agreeable to superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: To be agreeable to another, especially if he be above you, requires qualities that make you agreeable in respect to him — imitation of his faults, compliance or subservience to his vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such complaisance corrupts the client: he loses the virtue that could have enabled him to resent injury and often becomes morally compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common tricks of patrons to dismiss clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Patrons use arts of turning off dependants: expressions of sorrow for 'an unaccountable Accident', blaming obscure opponents, flattering whispers to suggest slowness in doing for a man's talents, and other devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise these evasions as strategic maneuvers that excuse inaction; be skeptical of patron apologies and of flattery that masks inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social risk of withdrawing after long attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: After long unprofitable attendance, when a man withdraws to pursue his own interests, it is often taken as ill-breeding and met with 'the pleasantest Insolence' by some who resent the withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware withdrawing may be criticized despite being the sensible course; weigh social cost against personal welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as disinterring latent virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is likened to sculpture: the figure (virtue) lies hid in the block (soul) and the art (education) clears away superfluous matter to bring the person forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper education draws out latent virtues and perfections that otherwise remain concealed; the writer endorses discourses of morality and reflection as primary means of improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of cultivating 'savage' virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues seen among 'savage' or uncultivated peoples (courage, resolution, fidelity) are admirable and, when rightly cultivated, could be raised to noble effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not despise natural virtues in other peoples; instead, aim to cultivate and direct passions with reason and moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of treating slaves with contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust that Negroes are treated with contempt: they are human beings deserving the common foot of humanity, protection under law, and prospects of happiness in this world and another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for legal and moral reforms: do not put only an insignificant fine on murder of slaves; deny neither civil nor spiritual means of happiness to enslaved persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions unregulated by reason produce horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of unregulated passions (the murder–suicide of lovers among slaves) show that without virtue and reason passions produce monstrous actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence the importance of education and moral discipline: violent or excessive passions need to be regulated to produce noble fruits rather than barbarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion about printing praise
rubrics_metrics.description: The author declines to publish many well-penned praises he receives because publishing them 'would...be a sufficient Instance to the World that I did not deserve them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid printing encomiums that would expose the author to appearing undeserving; exercise discretion about including praise to preserve integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club behaviour and discretion (She-Romps)
rubrics_metrics.description: A described female club indulges in romping, rudeness, tearing garments, and once a month 'demolish[es] a Prude' — a social custom of mocking formal women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator declines to attend, comparing himself to an intruder; implicit guidance: keep prudence and caution about attending wild private societies and maintain discretion about their rites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness/delicacy in speech and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Polite behaviour (termed 'Delicacy') entails refraining from coarse expressions and actions — e.g., speaking of being 'all over in a Sweat', saying 'my Stomach aked', complaining of something 'stuck in her Teeth', or eating fruit greedily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a person is to be suitable as a mistress or wife they should adopt these refinements; hints and gentle reproofs are the acceptable means to correct such uncouth behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame may be divided into three species: Glory (respects the Hero), Reputation (preserved by the Gentleman), and Credit (must be supported by every Tradesman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each species has different vulnerabilities: glory resists rumour, reputation is upheld by good behaviour and defence, credit is fragile and easily ruined by idle talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in speaking of merchants (protect credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a merchant's credit is vulnerable to casual whispers, one ought to be careful in language about merchants; speaking ill of a merchant can reduce plenty to want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never speak ill of a merchant except in a Court of Justice; recognise that a merchant's handwriting and credit are public goods and that careless calumny can cause ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: True quality vs. titles and honours
rubrics_metrics.description: True quality arises from Fortune, Body, or Mind (knowledge/virtue). Honours and titles often become marks of grandeur rather than merit and appear empty at death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct ambition toward virtue (the genuine source of honour) rather than transient worldly distinctions; act one's allotted part in life excellently rather than striving only for rank.
